title: Take a Number
concept: A Needham, Massachusetts company has asked FERC for a preliminary permit to study a proposed subsea data center in Cook Inlet, 66 seabed pods run by about 330 to 350 tidal turbines, about 100 megawatts and a 3.5 mile cable to Nikiski. The permit only lets the holder study the site and claim first place in line, and the company says it gives no permission to build. The objection deadline passed on November 2nd. The borough mayor called the approach sloppy and says he heard nothing, the company says it was too early, a fisheries alliance and a conservation group object, and the film gives the company's best case its own lemon room before narrowing: the question is not whether to study but who is in the room when the study is designed, with the 331 belugas drawn against the 1,300 of 1979 and kept apart from the fleet's 1,300 permits. Hero is a take-a-number machine and the throughline is ticket P-15423.

fingerprint.palette: blue-hour true violet shore, shingle slate, a vermilion dispenser, one acid lemon lamp for the Test, fleet blue permit tags and white beluga dots
fingerprint.metaphor: a take-a-number machine on the Nikiski shore: the permit is a place in line, and the film asks who else is handed a number before the study is written

palette: blue-hour true violet shore, shingle slate, a vermilion dispenser, one acid lemon lamp for the Test, fleet blue permit tags and white beluga dots
divergence_note: The last films were an oxblood courtroom (11-09), a permafrost road (11-08), a teal transformer yard (11-07), a tangerine office (11-06) and a midnight indigo cab (11-02), so the sky moves to a true violet. This film is a true violet blue-hour shore with a vermilion ticket machine, a seabed cross-section, a blue pegboard wall and one acid lemon lamp over a desk seen from above. It has no courtroom, cab, office or desk-chart, and its throughline is one ticket that is printed, stamped, parked, argued over and finally split in two.

treatment.title: Take a Number
treatment.summary: All four pitches converged on the take-a-number ticket, which carries the angle (order, not whether) in one object any Alaskan has stood in line for. The dramatist's shore dispenser and loop back to an empty queue gives the cleanest bookend. The explainer's dot field is the hardest-landing number drawn physical. The comedian's gags stay off the whales and the named people. The enthusiast supplies the fair upside so the Test scene reads as a case and not a strawman.

angle.thesis: The Cook Inlet fight isn't yet about whether a subsea AI data center belongs there. It's about order: DeepGreen claimed a place in line at FERC before it talked to the people who share the water, so the neighbors first met the project as a federal deadline.
angle.falsifier: False if the record shows DeepGreen did contact the borough before filing (contradicts c11), or if the objections would read the same with or without outreach, meaning they rest only on physical effects.

supporting_facts.fact: Both the FERC notice and DeepGreen agree the permit is study priority only, so the dispute can't be about what was filed.
The borough mayor calls it sloppy and says he heard nothing, DeepGreen says it was too early to reach out.
The first formal way to answer was a FERC window that closed November 2nd, and the fleet alliance and a conservation group used it.

angle.fair_counterpoint: A study permit is exactly the stage meant to produce the biology and engineering. Blocking it could mean nobody gathers the data, and nothing in the claims links the project to harm to belugas. DeepGreen's 'too early' is a defensible reading of how the system is designed.
angle.valence: mixed, constructive. The fix is cheap and Alaska-first: study and outreach run together. The idea of Alaska tidal power feeding compute stays worth studying.

second_movement.recontextualizing_fact: c14 to c16: belugas endangered since 2008, 331 whales now (290 to 386) versus about 1,300 in 1979. With so little room for error, who sets the study questions is the stake, and it is a different thing from the fleet's 1,300 permits (never blur the two numbers).
second_movement.test: Draw DeepGreen's best case at full strength as its own scene (study first is how you get answers, nothing built, nothing linked to whale harm), and let the film narrow honestly: the neighbors aren't asking for no study, they're asking to be in the room when the study is scoped.

runner_ups: process explainer alone (too procedural, no stakes)
physical-stakes alone (risks implying harm the claims don't support)
guardrails: c11 and c12 never in quotation marks
do not say Upper or narrowest
closing question seed: should the borough, the fleet and NOAA's beluga scientists help write the study terms before work starts

open_loop.what: Who else gets a number? Planted when a second ticket reading NEXT peeks from the slot, paid when three chairs slide up to the study table.

open_loop_2.what: Will the BUILD lever ever unlock? Planted when the lever is padlocked beside the dark LICENSE window, paid when the applicant tugs the lock in the company's best case and it holds with the window still dark.
